scenario: AITA for telling my SIL to shut up? | My SIL drives me a little bonkers sometimes. She is extremely proud of things like not watching TV, not listening to pop music, not having Facebook, and she interrupts conversations to say it. Often insulting the thing as well, instead of just saying that she doesn’t like it. Instead it’s about her superiority for not liking it. A few days ago we were having dinner and my 14-year-old sister starts talking about she watched a Marvel movie and she’s looking forward to a sequel that should be coming out soon. My SIL said, “I’ve never watched any Marvel movies. They seem pretty awful.” I was pissed off, I don’t get why my SIL, an adult woman, feels the need to be so rude and dismissive towards a teenager. I said loudly, “shut up, not everything has to be about you and what you like.” She blushed and didn’t say anything more, my brother didn’t say anything either. But he messaged me after they left saying that this was my expression of “always hating” his wife and that I’m a bad person who doesn’t want her to participate in conversation. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to tell my SIL (sister-in-law) to "shut up" during dinner. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, my SIL drives me a little bonkers sometimes. She's really proud of not watching TV, not listening to pop music, and not having Facebook. She always interrupts conversations to mention these things, and instead of just saying she doesn't like them, she makes it about her superiority for not liking them. That's pretty annoying. A few days ago, we were having dinner, and my 14-year-old sister started talking about a Marvel movie she watched and was looking forward to the sequel. My SIL jumped in and said she's never watched any Marvel movies and that they seem pretty awful. I got really pissed off because I don't understand why my SIL feels the need to be so rude and dismissive towards a teenager. So, I loudly told her to "shut up," adding that not everything has to be about her and what she likes. She blushed and didn't say anything more, and my brother didn't say anything either. But later, he messaged me saying that this was my expression of always hating his wife and that I'm a bad person who doesn't want her to participate in conversations. Now, I'm wondering if I did the right thing or not. On one hand, I was standing up for my sister and trying to shut down my SIL's rude behavior. On the other hand, telling someone to "shut up" is pretty harsh, and it might have made things worse between me and my SIL, especially since my brother is now upset with me. I need to think about the consequences of my actions. Did I handle the situation in the best way possible? Could there have been a better way to address my SIL's behavior without resorting to telling her to "shut up"? Also, how does this affect my relationship with my brother and SIL moving forward? Maybe I should consider alternative ways to deal with my SIL's interruptions and rude comments. Instead of confronting her directly in front of everyone, perhaps I could talk to her privately about how her comments make me feel. That way, I can express my feelings without making her feel attacked or embarrassed. Additionally, I should think about why my SIL behaves this way. Is she trying to assert her independence or maybe she feels insecure about her choices? Understanding her perspective might help me respond more compassionately rather than reacting impulsively. I also need to reflect on how my actions impact my brother. He seems to have taken my comment personally and is now upset with me. This could strain our relationship, which is something I don't want. Maybe I should apologize to him and explain my intentions, so he understands that my actions were not meant to hurt him or his wife. In summary, while I felt justified in standing up for my sister and addressing my SIL's rude behavior, the way I did it might have been counterproductive. It's important to consider alternative approaches that are more constructive and respectful, both for maintaining healthy relationships and for effectively addressing the issue at hand.
